curriculum: NMC Competency-Based MCh Neurosurgery Curriculum / NBEMS NEET-SS Surgical Group (Neurosurgery)
examPattern: NEET-SS Surgical Group paper (150 MCQs, 40 percent feeder MS General Surgery and 60 percent super-speciality). Within the super-speciality share, neurosurgery carries about 12 to 16 questions: neurotrauma with GCS and CT decision-making, aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage and intracerebral bleed scores and thresholds, common brain tumours with Stupp and Simpson facts, hydrocephalus with tap-test and shunt facts, degenerative and traumatic spine with TLICS and ASIA facts, and Pott spine. Weight follows MCh Neurosurgery university papers (basic sciences, principles, recent advances), the INI-SS important-topic list and the exam-pyq overlays.
book: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd Edition 2025 (Elsevier) Chapter 41 for neurotrauma; Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple for applied anatomy; society guidelines (Brain Trauma Foundation, AHA/ASA, NCCN CNS, EANO, AANS/CNS, WFNS) for operative neurosurgery (no owned operative neurosurgery textbook: see SS-LESSONS-BOOK-GAPS.md)

modules.name: TBI Assessment, GCS and CT Decision Rules

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: The Glasgow Coma Scale sums eye opening 1 to 4, verbal response 1 to 5 and motor response 1 to 6 for a total of 3 to 15, and severe traumatic brain injury is a GCS of 8 or less, which is the standard threshold for intubation.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41; Brain Trauma Foundation TBI Guidelines 4e 2017

mustKnow.fact: Moderate head injury is a GCS of 9 to 12 and mild injury is 13 to 15, and any patient with a GCS of 8 or less after resuscitation needs an urgent noncontrast CT head plus neurosurgical referral.

NICE head injury guidance orders CT within 1 hour for GCS below 13 on arrival, GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury, suspected open or depressed or basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, or more than one episode of vomiting.

Anticoagulated patients with any loss of consciousness or amnesia after head injury also need a CT within 8 hours under NICE rules, because a normal examination does not exclude a surgical bleed on warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant.

The Marshall CT classification grades diffuse injury I to IV by cistern compression and midline shift, with V for an evacuated mass and VI for a non-evacuated mass, and higher grades carry stepwise higher mortality.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41; Marshall CT classification 1991

mustKnow.fact: The Rotterdam CT score refines Marshall by adding traumatic subarachnoid or intraventricular blood, an absent epidural mass lesion and the degree of shift, and it predicts 6 month outcome after moderate to severe injury.

Brain Trauma Foundation guidance places an intracranial pressure monitor when the post-resuscitation GCS is 3 to 8 with an abnormal CT, or with a normal CT plus two of age above 40 years, motor posturing, or systolic pressure below 90 mmHg.

A fixed dilated pupil on the side of the mass (Hutchinson pupil) signals uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve, while weakness on the same side as the mass is a false localising Kernohan notch of the opposite cerebral peduncle.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (herniation syndromes)

modules.name: Extradural Haematoma: Lucid Interval and Evacuation

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: Most extradural haematomas follow a tear of the middle meningeal artery under a temporal pterion fracture, and the classic course is a head injury with brief concussion, a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration as the clot expands.
CT shows a biconvex lens-shaped hyperdense collection that does not cross cranial suture lines because the dura is tacked down, unlike the crescent of a subdural haematoma that crosses sutures.
The swirl sign of mixed hyperdense clot with hypodense unclotted blood marks active bleeding and predicts expansion, and such patients go straight to theatre without delay for further imaging.

Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidance evacuates any extradural haematoma larger than 30 cubic cm regardless of GCS, because deterioration once the temporal lobe herniates is sudden and often fatal.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation Surgical Management of TBI 2006

mustKnow.fact: A GCS above 8 with a haematoma below 30 cubic cm, thickness below 15 mm and shift below 5 mm may be watched with serial CT and neurosurgical consultation, and any drop in GCS converts to surgery.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation Surgical Management of TBI 2006

mustKnow.fact: Craniotomy with clot evacuation and middle meningeal artery coagulation is the operation, with dural tenting sutures to close the extradural space, while a small burr hole is only a temporising measure in a peripheral centre.

Posterior fossa extradural haematoma is usually venous from a transverse or sigmoid sinus tear, and because the posterior fossa tolerates very little extra volume it is evacuated even when small if symptomatic or compressing the fourth ventricle.

Children develop extradural haematomas more readily because the dura is less adherent and the skull fractures easily, and a paediatric scalp haematoma with pallor and a falling haematocrit after minor trauma should prompt an urgent CT.

modules.name: Acute Subdural Haematoma: Bridging Veins and Craniotomy

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: Acute subdural haematoma follows tearing of bridging veins between cortex and dural sinuses during acceleration-deceleration, and it is commonest in elderly falls, assaults and anticoagulated patients with brain atrophy.
CT shows a hyperdense crescent along the hemisphere that crosses suture lines but not dural reflections such as the falx, which separates it from the lens-shaped extradural haematoma.

Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidance evacuates an acute subdural thicker than 10 mm or causing more than 5 mm of midline shift regardless of GCS, because the underlying brain swelling makes delay lethal.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation Surgical Management of TBI 2006

mustKnow.fact: Any GCS fall of 2 or more points, a fixed dilated pupil, or intracranial pressure above 20 mmHg in a comatose subdural patient also mandates urgent evacuation even when the clot measures below threshold.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation Surgical Management of TBI 2006

mustKnow.fact: The operation is a large trauma craniotomy with clot evacuation, bleeding cortical vessel control and lax duraplasty, leaving the bone flap off as a hemicraniectomy when the brain remains swollen.
Interhemispheric and posterior fossa acute subdurals deserve the same thresholds with a lower tolerance for observation, because venous bleeding there compresses deep structures early.
Acute subdural carries the worst prognosis of the extra-axial haematomas because the impact that tears veins also contuses cortex, so mortality exceeds extradural haematoma at every GCS band.

Reversal of coagulopathy runs parallel to theatre booking: 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and platelets plus desmopressin for antiplatelet-associated expansion.
mustKnow.source: AHA/ASA Spontaneous ICH Guideline 2022 (reversal principles applied to trauma)

modules.name: Chronic Subdural: Membranes, Burr Holes and Embolisation

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: Chronic subdural follows minor trauma weeks earlier in elderly, alcoholic or anticoagulated patients, when a liquefied clot with inner and outer membranes and fragile neovessels rebleeds repeatedly.
Presentation is fluctuating consciousness, headache, hemiparesis or new seizures rather than coma, and bilateral collections can cause a paradoxical quadriparesis with a deceptively good GCS.
CT shows a crescent that is hypodense when old, isodense to brain at 2 to 3 weeks when it is easiest to miss, and mixed density with septations when membranes and fresh blood coexist.

Symptomatic or thick chronic subdural with shift is washed out through one or two frontal-parietal burr holes with warm saline irrigation, and a closed subdural drain for 24 to 48 hours halves recurrence.
mustKnow.source: AANS/CNS chronic subdural guidance; Santarius drain trial 2009

mustKnow.fact: Twist-drill bedside drainage suits frail high-risk patients while craniotomy with membranectomy is reserved for organised, calcified or multiply recurrent collections with solid membranes.

Middle meningeal artery embolisation devascularises the outer membrane and is now the standard adjunct for recurrent, bilateral or high-risk surgical collections after the EMBOLISE and STEM trial readouts.
Routine dexamethasone is avoided after Dex-CSDH showed worse functional outcomes with steroids, and routine statins or tranexamic acid are not first-line outside trials.
Postoperative pneumocephalus with a flat head-end for a day, early mobilisation, prompt drain removal and resumption of anticoagulation within days balance recurrence against thromboembolism.

modules.name: Contusion, Diffuse Axonal Injury and Concussion

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: Cerebral contusions cluster at frontal and temporal poles from coup-contrecoup impact against the skull base, and they blossom over 24 to 48 hours, so repeat CT is mandatory when consciousness dips.

Diffuse axonal injury follows high-speed deceleration with immediate prolonged coma but a deceptively normal early CT, and MRI susceptibility sequences later show microbleeds at the grey-white junction, corpus callosum and dorsolateral midbrain.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41; AANS/CNS severe TBI imaging guidance

mustKnow.fact: The Adams grading of diffuse axonal injury runs from grey-white junction lesions to corpus callosum involvement to dorsolateral brainstem lesions, with brainstem lesions carrying the worst prognosis.
Concussion is a functional injury with no CT or routine MRI abnormality, diagnosed clinically by headache, fogginess, imbalance and delayed recall after biomechanical energy transfer to the brain.

Return to play and learning follows a stepwise protocol with at least 24 hours per step and medical clearance, and any second impact before recovery risks catastrophic second-impact syndrome in adolescents.
Post-concussion symptoms beyond 4 weeks in adults merit supervised active rehabilitation and vestibular therapy rather than prolonged dark-room rest, which worsens outcomes.
Cerebral fat embolism after long-bone fractures mimics diffuse axonal injury with coma, hypoxia and petechiae, but MRI shows a starfield pattern and the history of trauma timing gives it away.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (white matter injury patterns)

mustKnow.fact: Post-traumatic epilepsy risk is highest with depressed fractures, intracerebral haematomas and prolonged amnesia, and one week of phenytoin or levetiracetam after severe injury prevents early but not late seizures.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation TBI Guidelines 4e 2017; Temkin seizure trial 1990

modules.name: Skull Fractures and CSF Rhinorrhoea

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 41 (Emergency care of neurologic injuries)

mustKnow.fact: A simple linear vault fracture with intact neurology needs no surgery, only observation and a CT to exclude an underlying extradural haematoma that can evolve over hours.

Depressed fractures are elevated when depression exceeds the thickness of the adjacent skull, when bone is contaminated through a scalp laceration, or when fragments compress eloquent cortex or cause a leak.
Compound fractures need urgent washout, debridement, tetanus cover and broad antibiotics covering skin flora plus gram negatives, because infection risk rises steeply after 8 hours of exposure.

Growing fractures strike children below 3 years when a dural tear lets arachnoid herniate into the fracture line, forming a pulsatile leptomeningeal cyst that widens the gap and needs dural repair with cranioplasty.

Base-of-skull fractures declare themselves through periorbital raccoon eyes, postauricular Battle sign, haemotympanum, otorrhoea or rhinorrhoea, and anosmia or facial palsy localises the anterior or temporal fracture line.
Post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea is confirmed at the bedside by the halo ring sign and in the laboratory by beta 2 transferrin, which is specific to CSF, perilymph and vitreous.

Most traumatic leaks stop within 7 to 10 days with head elevation, stool softeners, acetazolamide and a lumbar drain, while leaks persisting beyond 2 weeks or any meningitis episode mandate endoscopic or open skull base repair.

Tension pneumocephalus with the Mount Fuji sign of compressed frontal lobes and widened interhemispheric air is a neurosurgical emergency needing burr-hole air release, usually through the same frontal sinus or fracture defect.

modules.name: Raised ICP: Monro-Kellie and Tiered Therapy

topics.book: Brain Trauma Foundation TBI Guidelines 4e 2017 (tiered ICP therapy)

mustKnow.fact: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that blood, brain and CSF share a fixed vault volume, so any new mass first displaces CSF and venous blood and then raises pressure steeply once compensation is exhausted.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (intracranial compartments)

mustKnow.fact: Brain Trauma Foundation guidance treats sustained intracranial pressure above 22 mmHg because values beyond this threshold independently predict death and poor recovery after severe injury.
Cerebral perfusion pressure is held at 60 to 70 mmHg, avoiding below 50 and prolonged above 70 with aggressive fluids and pressors, since both ischaemia and ARDS-like lung injury worsen outcome.

First-tier measures are 30 degree head elevation with a neutral neck, adequate analgesia and propofol sedation, fever control, seizure control and CSF drainage through a ventricular catheter, which both monitors and treats.
Hyperosmolar therapy uses 3 percent hypertonic saline boluses or mannitol 0.25 to 1 g per kg, preferring saline when systolic pressure is borderline and watching serum sodium and osmolarity ceilings.

Brief hyperventilation to a carbon dioxide of 30 to 35 is only a bridge to definitive evacuation, and prophylactic hyperventilation below that range in the first 24 hours is forbidden because it causes ischaemia.

High-dose barbiturates with burst-suppression monitoring control refractory pressure but drop blood pressure and immunity, steroids worsen death after CRASH, and prophylactic hypothermia is not routine after Eurotherm.
mustKnow.source: Brain Trauma Foundation TBI Guidelines 4e 2017; CRASH trial 2004; Eurotherm3235 trial 2015

mustKnow.fact: Early enteral nutrition within 72 hours, chemical DVT prophylaxis once the CT is stable, and daily awakening with delirium screening complete the ICU bundle around pressure control.

modules.name: Decompressive Craniectomy and Cranioplasty

topics.book: RESCUEicp and DECRA trial readouts (decompressive surgery indications)

mustKnow.fact: Decompressive craniectomy is last-tier therapy for refractory intracranial pressure above 22 to 25 mmHg despite first and second tier measures, and RESCUEicp showed it lowers mortality at the price of more vegetative and dependent survivors.
Early bifrontal craniectomy for moderate pressure without a mass lesion worsened outcomes in DECRA, so surgery waits for truly refractory pressure rather than being done prophylactically.
Primary craniectomy at clot evacuation is the operating surgeon's choice for swollen brains with effaced cisterns, trading a second operation for immediate compliance and fewer ICU pressure crises.
The bone flap must span at least 12 by 15 cm with a stellate dural opening to the skull base, because a small craniectomy strangulates herniating brain at its edges.

Post-craniectomy hydrocephalus, subdural hygromas and epilepsy are watched for, and a sinking skin flap with headache, neglect or hemiparesis marks the syndrome of the trephined, which cranioplasty reverses.

Cranioplasty follows at 6 weeks to 3 months once swelling settles and infection is excluded, using banked autologous bone, titanium mesh, PEEK or acrylic, with temporalis preservation for cosmesis and chewing.
Children resorb banked bone flaps readily, so titanium or custom implants are preferred after large decompressions in the growing skull.
Bone flap infection or osteomyelitis needs flap removal, 6 weeks of culture-directed antibiotics and delayed synthetic cranioplasty, never immediate replacement of infected bone.

sections.name: Vascular Neurosurgery: Aneurysms, ICH and Malformations

modules.name: Aneurysmal SAH: Thunderclap, WFNS and Fisher

topics.book: AHA/ASA Guideline for Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Haemorrhage 2023

mustKnow.fact: Ruptured aneurysm presents with a thunderclap headache peaking within seconds, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and loss of consciousness, and a milder sentinel leak headache days earlier occurs in a third of patients.

The WFNS scale grades SAH by GCS plus focal deficit from I (GCS 15) to V (GCS 3 to 6 with deficit), and the Hunt-Hess scale runs I to V from mild headache to coma, both predicting outcome and timing of surgery.
mustKnow.source: AHA/ASA Aneurysmal SAH Guideline 2023; WFNS SAH Scale 1988

mustKnow.fact: The modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm from the CT blood load: thin SAH without ventricular blood is lowest risk while thick cisternal blood with intraventricular blood carries the highest delayed ischaemia risk.

About 30 percent of aneurysms sit at the anterior communicating artery, with posterior communicating and middle cerebral bifurcation next, and risk factors are smoking, hypertension, family history and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

Noncontrast CT is near perfect within 6 hours of onset but sensitivity falls after a day, so a negative late CT with strong suspicion needs lumbar puncture showing xanthochromia after 12 hours or CTA.

CTA is the first-line vessel study on a positive CT while DSA remains the gold standard for small, blister and treatment-planning detail, and every SAH gets vessel imaging urgently to find the bleeder.

Rebleeding risk peaks in the first 24 hours with mortality above 50 percent per rebleed, so the aneurysm is secured as early as feasible and blood pressure is controlled without dropping cerebral perfusion.

Acute hydrocephalus from intraventricular blood with a falling GCS needs an external ventricular drain, and chronic communicating hydrocephalus later needs a permanent shunt in about a fifth of survivors.

modules.name: Vasospasm and Delayed Cerebral Ischaemia after SAH

topics.book: AHA/ASA Guideline for Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Haemorrhage 2023

mustKnow.fact: Vasospasm begins around day 4, peaks at days 7 to 10 and resolves by day 21, and delayed cerebral ischaemia is a new focal deficit or infarct in that window not explained by hydrocephalus, seizures or infection.

Transcranial Doppler screening tracks middle cerebral artery velocities, with a mean above 120 cm per second suggesting spasm and above 200 or a Lindegaard ratio above 3 marking severe spasm needing escalation.

Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days is the only drug proven to improve outcome after aneurysmal SAH, and hypotension during dosing is managed with fluids and pressors rather than stopping the drug.

Triple H therapy is abandoned: euvolemia is the fluid goal, prophylactic hypervolemia and haemodilution do not prevent ischaemia, and induced hypertension with norepinephrine is reserved for symptomatic vasospasm with a secured aneurysm.

Refractory vasospasm goes to the angiosuite for intra-arterial verapamil or nicardipine and balloon angioplasty of proximal vessels, which durably dilates the basilar and proximal anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is usually cerebral salt wasting with hypovolemia and high urine sodium, treated with salt tablets or fludrocortisone, unlike SIADH which is euvolemic and fluid restricted.
Seizure prophylaxis is considered for high-risk SAH with a middle cerebral aneurysm, intracerebral haematoma or poor grade, but routine long-term antiepileptics are not continued without seizures.
Fever, anaemia and hyperglycaemia in the vasospasm window are all treated aggressively because each independently raises delayed ischaemia and infarction risk.

modules.name: Clipping versus Coiling and Flow Diversion

topics.book: ISAT and BRAT trial readouts; AHA/ASA Aneurysmal SAH Guideline 2023

mustKnow.fact: ISAT randomised ruptured anterior circulation aneurysms suitable for either treatment and found coiling gave better 1 year independent survival, at the cost of higher late rebleed and retreatment rates than clipping.

BRAT confirmed equipoise with crossover allowed, and real-world practice now coils most ruptured aneurysms while clipping favours middle cerebral bifurcation haematomas, wide necks and young patients needing durability.
Clipping runs through a pterional craniotomy with temporary parent clipping, permanent clip across the neck, and intraoperative Doppler or indocyanine green check of parent and branch patency.

Simple coiling fills the sac with detachable platinum coils, while stent-assisted coiling and balloon remodelling hold coils in wide-neck aneurysms and mandate dual antiplatelets when a stent is left.
Flow diverters such as the Pipeline device reconstruct large or fusiform internal carotid aneurysms from inside, with 6 months of dual antiplatelets and occlusion maturing over a year.
The WEB intrasaccular device treats wide-neck bifurcation aneurysms without dual antiplatelets, suiting ruptured middle cerebral and anterior communicating aneurysms with branch vessels at the neck.
mustKnow.source: WEB device literature; AHA/ASA Aneurysmal SAH Guideline 2023

mustKnow.fact: Unruptured aneurysms above 7 mm, posterior circulation location, daughter sacs and young age favour treatment, while small incidental anterior aneurysms in the elderly are usually watched with serial MRA under ISUIA principles.
Wrapping or coating is only a salvage when neither clip nor coil can hold, because wrapped aneurysms rebleed, and giant thrombosed aneurysms may need bypass with parent vessel sacrifice.

modules.name: Spontaneous ICH: Score, Pressure and Reversal

topics.book: AHA/ASA Guideline for Spontaneous Intracerebral Haemorrhage 2022

mustKnow.fact: Hypertensive bleeds favour the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, while strictly lobar bleeds in the elderly point to cerebral amyloid angiopathy under modified Boston criteria.
The ICH score sums GCS, haematoma volume above or below 30 mL, intraventricular blood, infratentorial origin and age above 80, giving 30 day mortality from near zero at 0 to near total at 5 to 6.
A CTA spot sign of contrast pooling inside the haematoma marks active bleeding and expansion risk, and such patients get the tightest pressure control and earliest repeat CT.
INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 support lowering systolic pressure below 140 mmHg within hours of a small to moderate bleed, avoiding drops below 110 to 120 that risk perihaematomal ischaemia.

Warfarin bleeds are reversed with 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K, dabigatran with idarucizumab, and factor Xa inhibitors with andexanet alfa or 4 factor concentrate when andexanet is unavailable.
PATCH showed platelet transfusion worsens outcome in antiplatelet-associated ICH without planned surgery, so platelets are reserved for operative cases, while desmopressin is a bedside adjunct.
TICH-2 found tranexamic acid does not improve function after ICH, and statins are continued rather than stopped, since withdrawal raises vascular events.

Continuous EEG is ordered for low GCS or cortical bleeds to catch nonconvulsive seizures, DVT prophylaxis starts with stockings and pumps with heparin added after 24 to 48 hours of stability, and dysphagia screening precedes any oral intake.

modules.name: ICH Surgery, Cerebellar Bleeds and Malignant Stroke

topics.book: STICH, MISTIE III and ENRICH trial readouts; AHA/ASA ICH Guideline 2022

mustKnow.fact: STICH I and II found no general functional benefit from early open evacuation of supratentorial ICH, so routine craniotomy for deep hypertensive bleeds is not done and surgery is individualised.
MISTIE III showed minimally invasive catheter evacuation with alteplase lowers mortality without improving function, keeping the technique for trial-selected lobar clots rather than routine use.
ENRICH showed early parafascicular minimally invasive evacuation within 24 hours improves function for lobar bleeds, making small-tube trans-sulcal surgery the modern option for accessible clots.

Cerebellar haematomas above 3 cm, with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus from fourth ventricular obstruction, go for suboccipital craniectomy plus external ventricular drainage without waiting for coma.

CLEAR III found alteplase irrigation of intraventricular blood through an EVD lowers mortality but not function, so it is offered for small parenchymal clots with massive ventricular blood causing obstruction.

Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction with more than 50 percent territory oedema and midline shift needs hemicraniectomy within 48 hours, which triples survival with independence in patients below 60 years per DECIMAL, DESTINY and HAMLET.
Above 60 years hemicraniectomy still saves life per DESTINY II but most survivors stay dependent, so the family discussion explicitly trades survival against likely dependency.

Decompressive surgery for posterior circulation stroke follows the same mass-effect logic as cerebellar bleeds: effaced quadrigeminal cisterns or hydrocephalus trigger suboccipital decompression plus drainage.

modules.name: Brain AVMs: Spetzler-Martin Grading and ARUBA

topics.book: Spetzler-Martin grading; ARUBA trial readout

mustKnow.fact: The Spetzler-Martin grade sums size below 3 cm as 1, 3 to 6 cm as 2 and above 6 cm as 3, plus 1 each for eloquent location and deep venous drainage, giving grades I to V with VI for inoperable lesions.

Grades I and II are surgical lesions with high cure and low morbidity, grade III is borderline multimodality territory, and grades IV and V are usually watched unless ruptured with a life-threatening haematoma.

ARUBA randomised unruptured AVMs and found medical management superior to intervention over about 3 years of follow-up (mean 33 months), so incidental unruptured malformations are generally observed while ruptured ones are treated.
Annual rupture risk is 2 to 4 percent, rising with prior rupture, deep or posterior fossa location and associated flow aneurysms, which are secured first when they bleed.
Radiosurgery obliterates deep or eloquent AVMs over 2 to 5 years with a latency bleed risk during the wait, and it suits lesions below 3 cm with compact nidus best.
Onyx embolisation cures only small selected niduses alone and otherwise shrinks lesions before surgery or radiosurgery, with staged sessions to avoid normal perfusion pressure breakthrough.
Seizures from an unruptured accessible AVM in eloquent-adjacent cortex may justify resection for epilepsy control, while deep asymptomatic lesions stay observed.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia with multiple AVMs needs family screening and lung AVM evaluation, since pulmonary shunts cause brain abscess and stroke. Wyburn-Mason patterns are sporadic and non-familial.

modules.name: Cavernomas and Dural Fistulas

topics.book: AANS/CNS cavernoma and dural fistula guidance

mustKnow.fact: Cavernomas show a popcorn core of blood products with a dark hemosiderin rim on MRI, enhance minimally, and hide on angiography, which separates them from AVMs and tumours.
Zabramski MRI types run from acute haemorrhage to calcified burnt-out lesions, and a developmental venous anomaly alongside is left alone because resecting it infarcts draining brain.
Familial cavernomas with CCM1 KRIT1, CCM2 or CCM3 mutations present with multiple lesions, and relatives get gradient-echo MRI screening plus spinal imaging when symptomatic.
A single accessible cavernoma causing epilepsy is resected with its hemosiderin rim for seizure control, while deep asymptomatic ones are watched because each bleed is usually small.
Brainstem cavernomas are operated only after two symptomatic bleeds via a safe entry zone approach, balancing rebleed risk against certain new deficit.

Dural arteriovenous fistulas present with pulsatile tinnitus, orbital congestion or haemorrhage, and the Borden and Cognard scales grade danger by cortical venous reflux, with reflux mandating treatment.

Transverse-sigmoid fistulas without reflux may be watched, while reflux-positive fistulas are closed transarterially through the middle meningeal feeder, transvenously, surgically or with radiosurgery.
Carotid-cavernous fistulas cause chemosis, proptosis, bruit and ophthalmoplegia, and direct high-flow types after trauma need urgent endovascular closure to save vision.

modules.name: Moyamoya Disease and Cerebral Venous Thrombosis

topics.book: AHA Moyamoya and cerebral venous thrombosis guidance; EAN CVST Guideline

mustKnow.fact: Moyamoya shows bilateral terminal carotid stenosis with a puff-of-smoke collateral network on angiography, graded Suzuki I to VI, and RNF213 mutation links the East Asian familial form.
Children present with ischaemic strokes or TIAs triggered by crying and hyperventilation, while adults bleed from fragile collaterals, so presentation alone often suggests the age group.
Revascularisation combines direct STA to MCA bypass with indirect EDAS or muscle synangiosis, and anaesthesia avoids hyperventilation, hypotension and crying that precipitate ischaemia.
Associations include Down syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, sickle cell disease and thyroid disease, and unilateral early disease is watched closely because most cases progress bilaterally.

Cerebral venous thrombosis strikes young women on oral contraceptives, pregnancy, postpartum or dehydration with headache, seizures and papilloedema, and haemorrhagic infarcts that do not respect arterial territories.
mustKnow.source: EAN Guideline on Cerebral Venous Thrombosis 2017

mustKnow.fact: The empty delta sign on contrast CT and loss of flow void with sinus hyperintensity on MRI-MRV confirm thrombosis of the superior sagittal or transverse sinuses.
mustKnow.source: EAN Guideline on Cerebral Venous Thrombosis 2017

mustKnow.fact: Heparin or low molecular weight heparin is started even when the infarct has haemorrhagic transformation, followed by warfarin for 3 to 12 months, with dabigatran an alternative after RESPECT-CVT.
mustKnow.source: EAN Guideline on Cerebral Venous Thrombosis 2017; RESPECT-CVT 2019

mustKnow.fact: Endovascular thrombectomy or local thrombolysis is rescue therapy for deterioration despite heparin, and decompressive hemicraniectomy saves life when a large venous infarct herniates.
mustKnow.source: EAN Guideline on Cerebral Venous Thrombosis 2017

modules.name: Glioblastoma: Stupp Protocol and MGMT

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025; EANO Glioblastoma Guideline 2023

mustKnow.fact: WHO 2021 defines glioblastoma as IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic glioma with microvascular proliferation or necrosis, or TERT, EGFR or chromosome 7/10 molecular alterations even without those histology features.

MRI shows an irregular ring-enhancing frontal or temporal mass with central necrosis, surrounding oedema and butterfly spread across the corpus callosum, unlike the homogeneous enhancement of lymphoma.
Maximal safe resection with 5-ALA fluorescence and awake mapping for eloquent lesions extends survival, and surgery also provides MGMT methylation and NGS profiling that direct chemoradiation.
The Stupp protocol gives 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide 75 mg per sq m daily, then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide 150 to 200 mg per sq m on days 1 to 5 every 28 days.
MGMT promoter methylation predicts temozolomide benefit and longer survival, so methylated elderly patients get combined treatment while unmethylated frail patients may get radiotherapy alone.
Elderly or poor-performance patients receive hypofractionated 40 Gy in 15 fractions with temozolomide per the Perry regimen, balancing survival against treatment burden.

Tumour-treating fields add survival in newly diagnosed disease per EF-14, bevacizumab controls oedema and radiation necrosis without extending survival, and lomustine is the standard recurrence chemotherapy.
Pseudoprogression within 3 months of chemoradiation mimics recurrence on MRI, and perfusion rCBV plus MR spectroscopy choline peaks help separate it from true progression before changing therapy.

modules.name: Low-Grade Glioma, Oligodendroglioma and IDH

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025; EANO Low-Grade Glioma Guideline

mustKnow.fact: IDH mutation with 1p19q codeletion defines oligodendroglioma, IDH mutation with ATRX and TP53 loss defines astrocytoma, and IDH-wildtype low-grade histology behaves aggressively and is managed as high grade.
Oligodendrogliomas calcify in most cases with a fried-egg honeycomb histology and chicken-wire vessels, and frontal location with calcification on CT is the classic exam image.
RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951 proved radiotherapy plus PCV chemotherapy doubles survival in codeleted tumours, making PCV the regimen of choice for high-risk oligodendroglioma.
The RTOG high-risk definition is age above 40 or any subtotal resection, and such low-grade gliomas get adjuvant radiotherapy plus chemotherapy rather than observation.
Gross total resection improves survival and seizure control and is pursued with mapping when feasible, while eloquent residual disease is watched or irradiated based on molecular risk.
Vorasidenib, a brain-penetrant IDH inhibitor, delays progression in grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma after surgery per INDIGO, opening targeted therapy for young observed patients.
Seizures are the presenting symptom in most low-grade gliomas and levetiracetam is first-line, with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics avoided during chemotherapy because of interactions.
Malignant transformation declares itself with new enhancement, rising choline and clinical deterioration, prompting re-resection and molecular retesting for CDKN2A loss and higher grade.

modules.name: Meningioma: Dural Tail and Simpson Grades

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025; EANO Meningioma Guideline 2021

mustKnow.fact: Meningiomas are dural-based extra-axial masses with a dural tail, homogeneous enhancement, hyperostosis of adjacent bone and a CSF cleft, separating them from intra-axial gliomas on MRI.
WHO grades run 1 benign, 2 atypical with 4 to 19 mitoses or brain invasion, and 3 anaplastic with 20 or more mitoses, and grade drives adjuvant decisions more than size.
Simpson grades record resection completeness from I (tumour, dura and bone removed) to V (biopsy), and Simpson I of a convexity meningioma is effectively curative.

Skull base meningiomas of the olfactory groove, sphenoid wing and petroclival region accept planned subtotal resection with radiosurgery to the cavernous or petrous remnant to preserve cranial nerves.
Adjuvant radiotherapy follows subtotal or recurrent grade 2 disease and all grade 3 tumours per ROAM and EORTC 22042 principles, while fully resected grade 1 needs only surveillance MRI.
Spinal meningiomas favour the thoracic dura in middle-aged women with psammoma bodies, and Simpson I resection through a posterior approach usually cures back pain and myelopathy.
Multiple meningiomas with bilateral vestibular schwannomas mark NF2 with merlin loss, and family members need craniospinal screening.
Optic nerve sheath meningiomas present with painless visual loss and optic disc swelling with a tram-track sign, and they are irradiated rather than resected because surgery blinds.

modules.name: Vestibular Schwannoma: Koos Grade and Hearing

topics.book: AANS/CNS Vestibular Schwannoma Guideline; EANO Skull Base Guidance

mustKnow.fact: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance is the classic triad, and MRI shows an ice-cream-cone enhancing mass centred on the internal auditory canal with canal flaring.
Koos grades I to IV track size and brainstem contact from purely intracanalicular to brainstem compression with fourth ventricular shift, guiding observation versus treatment.
Gardner-Robertson classes record preoperative hearing, and serviceable hearing entering treatment decides between hearing-preservation retrosigmoid surgery, middle fossa surgery or radiosurgery.
Lesions below 1.5 cm in the elderly are observed with serial MRI because most do not grow, and growth or brainstem compression converts observation to treatment.
Stereotactic radiosurgery with 12 to 13 Gy marginal dose controls tumours below 3 cm with the best hearing preservation, at the price of delayed facial spasm risk and rare malignant transformation.

The retrosigmoid approach preserves hearing for larger tumours, translabyrinthine surgery sacrifices hearing for the best facial nerve outcomes in large lesions, and middle fossa suits small intracanalicular tumours with good hearing.
Facial nerve preservation outranks total resection, so planned subtotal resection with radiosurgery to the facial-adherent remnant is standard for large tumours.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2, where bevacizumab can restore hearing and cochlear or brainstem implants rehabilitate deafened ears after bilateral treatment.

modules.name: Pituitary Surgery: Acromegaly and Cushing Disease

topics.book: Endocrine Society Acromegaly Guideline 2014; Endocrine Society Cushing Guideline 2015

mustKnow.fact: Acromegaly screening starts with IGF-1, and failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 ng per mL on oral glucose tolerance testing confirms autonomous secretion from a somatotroph adenoma.
Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy is first-line for acromegaly, with surgical cure defined as normal age-matched IGF-1 plus random growth hormone below 1 ng per mL.
Persistent disease gets somatostatin analogues such as octreotide LAR, cabergoline for mild cases, and pegvisomant growth hormone receptor blockade with liver monitoring for resistant tumours.
Cushing disease is ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism from a corticotroph adenoma, screened with 1 mg overnight dexamethasone cortisol above 1.8 mcg per dL plus late-night salivary cortisol.
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with a central to peripheral ACTH ratio of 2 or more basally and 3 or more after CRH proves pituitary source and lateralises the adenoma side.

Selective transsphenoidal adenomectomy cures most microadenomas, with ketoconazole or metyrapone bridging severe hypercortisolism and bilateral adrenalectomy with lifelong Nelson surveillance as last resort.
Postoperative diabetes insipidus with the triphasic response and SIADH-like hyponatraemia around day 7 are watched with strict sodium monitoring after every transsphenoidal operation.
Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression, and urgent decompression is indicated for progressive visual loss even before complete endocrine workup.

modules.name: Prolactinoma, Apoplexy and Incidentaloma

topics.book: Endocrine Society Prolactinoma Guideline 2011; Pituitary Apoplexy UK Guidance 2021

mustKnow.fact: Prolactinoma is the commonest functional pituitary adenoma, presenting with amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and infertility in women and with macroadenoma mass effects in men.
Stalk compression hyperprolactinemia stays below 100 to 200 ng per mL, so higher values with a macroadenoma confirm true prolactinoma while modest rises need other causes excluded.
Cabergoline is first-line and shrinks most macroprolactinomas, with surgery reserved for drug resistance, intolerance, cystic components or visual compression unresponsive to dopamine agonists.
Rapid tumour shrinkage on cabergoline can open a CSF leak through an eroded skull base, so new rhinorrhoea on treatment needs urgent skull base assessment rather than simple drug stoppage.
Pituitary apoplexy presents with sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia, visual loss and adrenal crisis from haemorrhage into an adenoma, often precipitated by anticoagulation, surgery or dynamic testing.
Immediate high-dose hydrocortisone precedes all decisions in apoplexy, and urgent transsphenoidal decompression follows when visual acuity or fields are deteriorating.
Pituitary incidentalomas below 10 mm with normal hormones and vision are watched with MRI, while larger lesions get full pituitary panel plus formal visual fields.
Rathke cleft cysts are non-enhancing intrasellar cysts without calcification that mimic adenoma, and asymptomatic ones are observed while compressive ones are drained transsphenoidally.

modules.name: Craniopharyngioma and Suprasellar Lesions

topics.book: EANO Suprasellar and Craniopharyngioma Guidance; NCCN CNS Cancers 2025

mustKnow.fact: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma strikes children with cystic, calcified suprasellar masses and machine-oil cyst fluid driven by CTNNB1 mutations, while papillary type affects adults and carries BRAF V600E.
Calcified suprasellar cyst plus bitemporal hemianopia and growth failure in a child is craniopharyngioma until proven otherwise, separating it from pituitary adenoma and Rathke cyst.

Hypothalamic obesity, diabetes insipidus and panhypopituitarism dominate morbidity, so modern strategy favours safe subtotal resection with radiotherapy over hypothalamus-injuring gross total removal.
Papillary BRAF-mutant tumours respond to dabrafenib plus trametinib, allowing neoadjuvant shrinkage before conservative surgery in selected adults.
Cystic recurrences are managed through an Ommaya reservoir with intracavitary interferon alpha, deferring reoperation and radiotherapy in the growing child.
Proton radiotherapy is preferred for residual disease in children to spare cognition, hearing and the hypothalamic-pituitary axis compared with photon therapy.
Tuberculum sellae and planum meningiomas mimic craniopharyngioma but show a dural tail and homogeneous enhancement without calcified cysts, changing the approach to Simpson resection.
Lifelong endocrine, visual, sleep and neurocognitive surveillance follows every craniopharyngioma survivor, because late hypothalamic, vascular and second-tumour events are common.

modules.name: Brain Metastases, SRS and Spinal Mets

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025; AANS/CNS Brain Metastasis Guideline

mustKnow.fact: Metastases are the commonest brain tumours, arising from lung, breast, melanoma, renal and colorectal primaries, and multiple small round grey-white junction lesions with oedema suggest mets over glioma.
A large symptomatic or diagnostic-uncertain lesion is resected followed by cavity stereotactic radiosurgery, which controls the bed with less cognitive injury than whole-brain radiotherapy.
Gamma Knife radiosurgery with 12 to 24 Gy single-fraction marginal dose treats up to 4 lesions below 3 to 4 cm, and staged or fractionated SRS extends control to larger volumes.
Whole-brain radiotherapy is reserved for miliary disease and leptomeningeal spread, using hippocampal avoidance with memantine to limit memory loss.
Small-cell lung cancer with good response gets prophylactic cranial irradiation, while driver-mutated NSCLC and HER2 breast disease get CNS-penetrant systemic therapy alongside local control.
Graded prognostic assessment combines age, performance status, extracranial control and lesion count to select aggressive local therapy versus supportive care.

Spinal metastases are graded by SINS for instability and Bilsky ESCC for cord compression, and high-grade compression with instability gets separation surgery plus spine SBRT rather than radiotherapy alone.
Tokuhashi and Tomita scores estimate survival from primary type, visceral mets and neurology to choose en bloc excision, palliation or radiotherapy for spinal secondaries.

sections.name: Spine Surgery: Degenerative, Trauma and Infection

modules.name: Disc Prolapse: Dermatomes and Microdiscectomy

topics.book: AANS/CNS Lumbar Disc Herniation Guidance; NASS Clinical Guidelines

mustKnow.fact: Posterolateral L4-L5 and L5-S1 prolapses are commonest, compressing the traversing root so an L5-S1 disc hits S1 while a far-lateral disc hits the exiting root one level above.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (lumbosacral roots)

mustKnow.fact: L5 root pain runs to the dorsum of foot with weak dorsiflexion and extensor hallucis, while S1 pain runs to the lateral foot with weak plantarflexion and a lost ankle jerk.
Straight-leg raising below 60 degrees reproducing leg pain and a crossed positive test strongly predict a prolapse that matches the MRI level and side.
Red flags of retention, saddle numbness, bilateral sciatica or severe unremitting pain convert sciatica into an MRI emergency for cauda equina or infection or tumour.
Most prolapses improve within 6 to 12 weeks of analgesia, physiotherapy and graded return to work, and routine early MRI without red flags or deficit does not change management.
SPORT showed surgery relieves leg pain faster with equal long-term outcomes, so microdiscectomy is offered for persistent disabling sciatica beyond 6 weeks, progressive deficit or intolerable pain.
Modic endplate changes and high-intensity zones mark painful degenerative discs but do not mandate fusion alone, while sequestrated fragments migrating behind the body suit a targeted fragmentectomy.
Recurrent prolapse at the same level after 6 months gets redo discectomy, while instability, bilateral facetectomy or chronic axial pain push the decision toward fusion.

modules.name: Cauda Equina and Lumbar Canal Stenosis

topics.book: AANS/CNS Lumbar Stenosis Guidance; Cauda Equina standards (SBNS/BASS)

mustKnow.fact: Cauda equina syndrome presents with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, sexual dysfunction and micturition difficulty, and retention with overflow marks CES with retention needing the most urgent decompression.
Incomplete CES with altered urinary sensation but preserved voiding still needs emergency MRI and decompression within 24 to 48 hours, because delay converts bladder recovery from likely to unlikely.
A post-void residual above 200 mL with saddle numbness triggers the emergency pathway even when pain seems controlled, since painless retention is the classic missed presentation.
Wide laminectomy with discectomy is the operation, steroids have no role, and catheterisation with urology follow-up plus anal tone documentation completes the medicolegal record.
Lumbar canal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication with leg heaviness on standing and walking, relieved by sitting and by the flexed shopping-cart posture that opens the canal.
MRI shows the trefoil canal with facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum buckling and disc bulging, and vascular claudication is separated by pulse examination and relief with rest alone.
SPORT stenosis showed decompression improves pain and function over conservative care, with fusion added for degenerative spondylolisthesis, scoliosis or iatrogenic instability.
Interspinous spacers and indirect decompression suit frail claudicants without instability, while severe multilevel stenosis with deformity needs instrumented correction.

modules.name: Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy and OPLL

topics.book: AANS/CNS Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy Guideline 2017

mustKnow.fact: Degenerative cervical myelopathy presents with hand clumsiness, buttoning difficulty, unsteady gait and bladder urgency, with Hoffman, inverted brachioradialis, Babinski and Lhermitte signs on examination.
The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association score grades severity out of 17, with below 12 severe, 12 to 14 moderate and above 14 mild disease guiding surgical urgency.
Moderate, severe or progressive myelopathy is operated, while mild non-progressive disease is watched with serial mJOA and MRI because a fifth deteriorate.
Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion or corpectomy suits 1 to 2 level disease with kyphosis, while posterior laminoplasty or laminectomy-fusion suits multilevel stenosis with preserved lordosis.

Ossified posterior longitudinal ligament is common in East Asian patients and produces massive anterior compression, managed anteriorly by floating or resection and posteriorly when the canal occupancy is extreme.
MRI T2 hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity at the compressed level marks irreversible cord injury and predicts incomplete recovery, strengthening the case against delay.
Cervical radiculopathy with dermatomal arm pain and a positive Spurling test is managed like lumbar sciatica first, with foraminotomy or ACDF for persistent root deficit.
Postoperative C5 palsy with deltoid weakness, drip and dysphagia after anterior surgery, and hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal traction are the counselled complications.

modules.name: Spondylolisthesis, Meyerding and Fusion Choices

topics.book: AANS/CNS Lumbar Fusion Guideline; NASS Spondylolisthesis Coverage

mustKnow.fact: Meyerding grades slip as percent displacement from I below 25 to V above 100 percent spondyloptosis, and instability is significant slip progression or more than 3 to 4 mm motion on flexion-extension films.
Isthmic lysis from pars defects shows the Scotty dog collar on oblique views in young athletes, while degenerative L4-L5 slips with intact arch and stenosis affect elderly women.
Low-grade stable slips without stenosis are managed conservatively with bracing and core strengthening, and pars repair suits adolescents while fusion suits adults with pain or slip risk.
Fusion is indicated for instability, high-grade slip, recurrent prolapse with facetectomy, deformity and chronic axial pain with proven instability, not for uncomplicated first prolapse.

TLIF gives unilateral transforaminal access with one cage, PLIF gives bilateral access with more retraction, ALIF gives the largest lordotic cage anteriorly, and XLIF spares the back muscles through the psoas.
Smoking, diabetes and osteoporosis raise pseudoarthrosis risk, so cessation, glycaemic control and bone health optimisation precede elective fusion, with BMP reserved for high-risk cases.
Adjacent segment disease follows rigid fusion at about 2 to 3 percent per year, counselled preoperatively alongside dural tear, infection and hardware failure.
High-grade dysplastic slips in adolescents with L5 radiculopathy and hamstring tightness need reduction and instrumented fusion, never bracing alone.

modules.name: Thoracolumbar Trauma: Denis and TLICS

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 36 and 40 (trauma and musculoskeletal injuries)

mustKnow.fact: The Denis three-column model splits anterior, middle and posterior columns, and middle-column failure with retropulsion defines the unstable burst fracture that threatens the canal.

TLICS sums morphology with compression 1, burst 2, translation-rotation 3 and distraction 4, plus posterior ligamentous complex and neurology scores, with 5 or more favouring surgery and 3 or less bracing.
A burst fracture with an intact neurology and no PLC injury is braced in hyperextension, while progressive deficit, locked facet dislocation or open injury goes for urgent decompression and fixation.
Chance seat-belt fractures split the vertebra horizontally, with bony Chance healing in a brace and ligamentous Chance needing posterior tension-band fixation.
Ankylosing spondylitis and DISH spines snap like chalk sticks even after minor falls, and long-segment posterior fixation is needed because short constructs pull out of osteoporotic bone.

Osteoporotic wedge fractures without neurology are managed with analgesia, bracing and osteoporosis treatment, with vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty reserved for persistently painful non-healing fractures.

Log-rolling, pressure care and early fixation within 72 hours for unstable patterns reduce pulmonary and thrombotic complications of prolonged bed rest. Routine steroids have no role in acute spinal cord injury.
Post-traumatic kyphosis above 30 degrees, chronic pain or delayed deficit after a healed fracture merit late corrective osteotomy with instrumented fusion.

modules.name: Cervical Trauma, Odontoid and ASIA Syndromes

topics.book: AANS/CNS Cervical Spine Trauma and SCI Guidance; STASCIS readout

mustKnow.fact: Jefferson C1 burst fractures follow axial loading with lateral mass spread, and combined spread above 6.9 mm by the Rule of Spence marks transverse ligament rupture needing C1-C2 fusion.
Odontoid fractures are Anderson-DAlonzo type I tip, II base and III body, with type II in patients above 50 years or with posterior displacement favouring posterior C1-C2 fusion over a collar.
Hangman traumatic C2 spondylolisthesis from hyperextension-distraction is Levine-Edwards I to III, with types I and II collar-managed and IIa and III with severe angulation fixed at C2-C3.

Atlantoaxial instability with an atlantodental interval above 3 mm in adults or 5 mm in children, common in Down syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis, needs posterior C1 lateral mass to C2 pedicle fixation.
ASIA grades cord injury A complete through E normal, with the neurological level set by the lowest intact segment and sacral sparing distinguishing complete from incomplete injuries.

Central cord syndrome after elderly hyperextension gives weak arms with spared legs and sacral sensation, anterior cord gives paraplegia with lost pain but spared proprioception, and Brown-Sequard hemisection gives ipsilateral motor with contralateral pain loss.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (cord tracts)

mustKnow.fact: Mean arterial pressure is held at 85 to 90 mmHg for 7 days after acute cord injury per AANS/CNS guidance, while high-dose methylprednisolone is no longer routine after NASCIS reanalysis.

STASCIS supports decompression within 24 hours for cervical cord injury with ongoing compression, and neurogenic shock with hypotension plus bradycardia and warm skin is treated with fluids and vasopressors unlike hypovolemic shock.

modules.name: Pott Spine: Tuli Middle Path and ATT

topics.book: Tuli middle-path doctrine; NTEP spinal TB guidance; INDEX-TB readouts

mustKnow.fact: Tuberculosis reaches the paradiscal anterior vertebral body through Batson venous plexus, favouring lower thoracic and upper lumbar levels, with disc involvement distinguishing it from pyogenic sparing of the disc early.
Cold abscesses track along psoas shadows, paravertebral lines widen, pedicles erode late unlike tumour, skip lesions occur, and Gibbus deformity marks anterior collapse in children.

MRI shows subligamentous spread across levels with disc hyperintensity and rim-enhancing abscesses, and CT-guided biopsy with GeneXpert CBNAAT plus culture confirms diagnosis and rifampicin resistance.
NTEP and INDEX-TB treat drug-sensitive spinal TB with 2 months of HRZE then 10 months of HRE, a 12 month regimen with directly observed adherence and nutrition support.
Tuli middle path manages without surgery when there is no deficit, instability or deformity, using ATT with bracing and serial neurology, since most paradiscal disease heals medically.

Surgery is indicated for progressive deficit, spinal instability, severe kyphosis, no response after 3 to 6 months of ATT, or diagnostic doubt, via anterior debridement with strut graft plus posterior instrumentation.

The Hong Kong radical anterior debridement with rib strut grafting remains the gold standard for anterior disease with large abscesses, while pure posterior approaches suit limited posterior element disease.

Kyphosis above 60 degrees or progressing deformity in healed disease needs corrective osteotomy, and drug-resistant spine TB gets bedaquiline-based NTEP regimens with surgical debulking for load reduction.

modules.name: Intraspinal Tumours: Ependymoma, Schwannoma, Mets

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025 (spinal tumours); AANS/CNS Spinal Tumour Guidance

mustKnow.fact: Myxopapillary ependymomas of the filum present with low back pain and sphincter disturbance, and en bloc gross total resection is curative while piecemeal removal seeds the canal.

Intramedullary ependymomas sit centrally with a cap sign of polar haemosiderin and a clear plane, favouring gross total resection, unlike eccentric infiltrative astrocytomas that get biopsy plus radiotherapy.
Schwannomas arise from dorsal roots as enhancing dumbbell lesions widening the foramen, and large ones need facetectomy with instrumented fusion after resection to prevent deformity.
Thoracic spinal meningiomas with dural tails in middle-aged women are resected posteriorly with dural coagulation or patch, curing myelopathy in most cases.
Drop metastases from medulloblastoma and ependymoma coat the cord with sugar-coating enhancement, staged with full craniospinal MRI and CSF cytology at diagnosis.
Sacral chordomas and chondrosarcomas need wide en bloc spondylectomy because intralesional surgery recurs, with proton therapy for positive margins.
Ewing sarcoma of the spine gets neoadjuvant chemotherapy with EWSR1 testing then surgery plus radiotherapy, unlike adult metastases that get separation surgery plus SBRT.
Haemangioblastomas with flow voids and syrinx in VHL disease are resected curatively with devascularisation first, and family screening follows every VHL-associated lesion.

modules.name: Hydrocephalus Classification and NPH Triad

topics.book: ISPN Hydrocephalus Guidance; AANS/CNS Adult Hydrocephalus Guideline

mustKnow.fact: Obstructive hydrocephalus blocks CSF flow inside the ventricles, commonest at the aqueduct, while communicating hydrocephalus blocks absorption at arachnoid granulations after bleed or meningitis.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (ventricles and CSF flow)

mustKnow.fact: Choroid plexus papilloma overproduces CSF in children with a vividly enhancing frond-like ventricular tumour, cured by total resection that removes the source.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the wet, wobbly, wacky triad of incontinence, gait apraxia and dementia, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy on MRI.
Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid spaces (DESH) with tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle below 90 degrees mark shunt-responsive NPH imaging.
The tap test drains 40 to 50 mL of CSF with timed gait and cognitive testing before and after, and objective gait improvement predicts shunt response.
Aqueduct stenosis from tectal glioma or webs is treated by endoscopic third ventriculostomy rather than shunting, bypassing the block at the floor of the third ventricle.
Dandy-Walker malformation combines a posterior fossa cyst with vermian hypoplasia and elevated torcula, managed by shunting the cyst, the ventricles or both based on compartments.
Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity is temporised with ventricular reservoirs or drains, with permanent shunting only after CSF protein and infection settle.

modules.name: VP Shunts, ETV and Shunt Complications

topics.book: ISPN Hydrocephalus Guidance; VP shunt operative principles

mustKnow.fact: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting through Kocher or Keen entry remains first-line for communicating hydrocephalus, with programmable valves allowing transcutaneous pressure adjustment without revision.
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy fenestrates the tuber cinereum floor anterior to the mammillary bodies and posterior to the infundibulum, demanding respect for the basilar tip below.
The ETV success score combines age, aetiology and prior shunt history, predicting durable success best in older children with aqueduct stenosis or tectal tumours and no prior shunt.
Proximal obstruction from choroid or debris is commonest, presenting with headache, vomiting and a non-compressible reservoir, while distal failure presents with abdominal pseudocyst or peritonitis.
Shunt infection, usually Staph epidermidis within 6 months of surgery, needs complete hardware removal with external drainage plus antibiotics, never antibiotics alone through an infected shunt.
Overdrainage causes slit-ventricle syndrome, subdural collections and postural headache, managed by upgrading to programmable or anti-siphon valves rather than repeated shunt ligation.
Lumboperitoneal shunts suit communicating hydrocephalus and idiopathic intracranial hypertension but risk acquired Chiari from craniospinal pressure dissociation, so ventricles are checked serially.

Shunt independence is never assumed: a blocked shunt in a shunt-dependent adult is lethal within hours, so emergency drill cards, valve settings records and 24 hour neurosurgical access are counselled.

modules.name: Chiari, Syringomyelia and Craniovertebral Junction

topics.book: AANS/CNS Chiari and Syringomyelia Guidance; Goel CVJ doctrine

mustKnow.fact: Chiari I is tonsillar descent beyond 5 mm with a small posterior fossa, half with syringomyelia, presenting with occipital headache on coughing, downbeat nystagmus and hand wasting.
Symptomatic Chiari I with syrinx or brainstem compression gets foramen magnum decompression with duraplasty, while asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia is watched.
Chiari II accompanies myelomeningocele with a small posterior fossa, beaked tectum and medullary kinking, and most need shunting with decompression reserved for symptomatic brainstem compression.
Syringomyelia produces cape-like dissociated sensory loss with spared touch, intrinsic hand wasting, and painless Charcot joints from unfelt injuries.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (spinothalamic tract)

mustKnow.fact: Most syrinxes resolve after Chiari decompression restores cisternal flow, with direct syrinx shunting reserved for post-traumatic or post-infective loculated cavities.
Basilar invagination drives the odontoid above Chamberlain and McGregor lines into the foramen magnum, causing long-tract signs and lower cranial palsies that posterior reduction-fixation reverses.
Goel doctrine treats most basilar invagination as atlantoaxial instability, fixing C1-C2 posteriorly with joint distraction even without transoral odontoidectomy in reducible cases.
Traumatic atlanto-occipital dislocation per Traynelis patterns is highly lethal, and survivors get urgent occipitocervical fusion because the ligamentous injury never heals in a collar.

modules.name: Neural Tube Defects, MMC and Tethered Cord

topics.book: MOMS trial readout; AAP Spina Bifida Guidance; NTEP folate policy context

mustKnow.fact: Periconceptional folic acid 4 mg daily for high-risk and 0.4 mg for routine mothers prevents most neural tube defects, started at least a month before conception.
Myelomeningocele exposes the placode through defective skin and dura in the lumbosacral spine, leaking CSF and guaranteeing Chiari II, hydrocephalus and orthopaedic and bladder deficits.
The MOMS trial proved prenatal repair before 26 weeks halves shunt need and improves motor outcomes versus postnatal repair, at the price of prematurity and uterine dehiscence risk.
Postnatal closure within 48 hours with placode tubularisation, dural closure and skin cover prevents meningitis, followed by shunting when ventricles enlarge.
Tethered cord holds the conus below L2 with a thickened filum above 2 mm, presenting with back pain, foot deformity, scoliosis and new incontinence in a growing child.
Sectioning the filum through a limited laminotomy detethers the cord, while lipomyelomeningocele with intact skin gets prophylactic detethering before deficits appear.
Split cord malformation with a bony spur dividing hemicords needs spur resection with dural reconstruction plus detethering, since either half tethers growth.
Congenital dermal sinus tracts from failed dysjunction connect skin pits to the thecal sac and need complete tract excision, because retained epithelium seeds dermoids and meningitis.

modules.name: Paediatric Brain Tumours: Pilocytic, Medulloblastoma, DIPG

topics.book: NCCN CNS Cancers Guideline 2025 (paediatric tumours); WHO CNS 5e molecular groups

mustKnow.fact: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the commonest benign childhood tumour, a cerebellar cyst with an enhancing mural nodule driven by BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion, cured by gross total resection alone.
Medulloblastoma is a midline vermian tumour of childhood with truncal ataxia, molecular groups WNT best, SHH intermediate and groups 3 and 4 worst, staged with craniospinal MRI and CSF cytology.
Standard-risk medulloblastoma after maximal resection gets craniospinal irradiation with chemotherapy, while infants get chemotherapy-first strategies to defer radiation toxicity.

Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma presents with multiple cranial nerve palsies and ataxia, shows diffuse pontine expansion with H3K27M mutation, and gets radiotherapy only since resection is impossible.
Posterior fossa ependymoma splits into PFA infantile aggressive and PFB older indolent groups, and gross total resection plus focal radiotherapy is the standard.
Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumour strikes infants with SMARCB1 INI1 loss, demands intensive multimodal therapy, and is distinguished from medulloblastoma by genetics not imaging.
Posterior fossa syndrome with mutism, dysphagia and emotional lability follows vermian splitting, and most children recover speech over weeks to months with therapy.
Optic pathway gliomas in NF1 children are watched unless vision falls, since most are indolent pilocytic lesions and treatment threatens vision more than the tumour.

modules.name: CNS Infections: Abscess, TBM and NCC

topics.book: IDSA Brain Abscess and Encephalitis Guidance; RNTCP/NTEP CNS TB norms

mustKnow.fact: Brain abscess complicates otitis, sinusitis and cyanotic heart disease, and MRI shows ring enhancement with central diffusion restriction that separates pus from necrotic tumour.
Lesions above 2.5 cm, with mass effect, near ventricles or failing antibiotics get stereotactic aspiration, while small deep lesions and cerebritis get 6 to 8 weeks of ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.
Subdural empyema from sinusitis spreads rapidly over the hemisphere with seizures and deficits, needing emergent craniotomy washout plus sinus drainage because burr holes miss loculations.
Tuberculous meningitis gives basal exudates, hydrocephalus and infarcts with CSF showing high protein, low glucose and lymphocytic pleocytosis, confirmed by GeneXpert Ultra.
Dexamethasone plus 12 months of ATT with shunting for hydrocephalus is the TBM standard, and paradoxical worsening on treatment is managed medically not by abandoning ATT.
mustKnow.source: NTEP CNS TB Guidance; Thwaites dexamethasone trial 2004

mustKnow.fact: Neurocysticercosis shows the hole-with-dot scolex on MRI, single enhancing lesions with seizures get albendazole plus steroids, and intraventricular cysts need endoscopic removal before hydrocephalus kills.
Toxoplasmosis in HIV with CD4 below 100 gives multiple basal ganglia ring lesions treated with pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine, distinguished from lymphoma by thallium SPECT and treatment response.
Hydatid cysts are removed intact by the Dowling hydrostatic technique without rupture, since spillage seeds anaphylaxis and recurrence across the operative field.

modules.name: Epilepsy Surgery, Trigeminal Neuralgia and DBS

topics.book: AANS/CNS Epilepsy Surgery Guideline; ILAE drug-resistant epilepsy definition

mustKnow.fact: Drug-resistant epilepsy means failure of 2 appropriate antiepileptic schedules, and such patients are referred to comprehensive epilepsy surgery evaluation rather than endless drug rotations.
Mesial temporal sclerosis after febrile seizures causes refractory temporal lobe epilepsy, and anterior temporal lobectomy gives 60 to 70 percent seizure freedom versus continued medical therapy.
Selective amygdalohippocampectomy preserves language and memory better than full lobectomy for dominant-hemisphere MTS, chosen when neuropsychology predicts cognitive cost.

Stereo-EEG with depth electrodes maps non-lesional networks, vagal nerve stimulation palliates generalised epilepsies, corpus callosotomy stops drop attacks in Lennox-Gastaut, and hemispherotomy cures Rasmussen and Sturge-Weber children.
Trigeminal neuralgia from superior cerebellar artery compression gives electric shock V2-V3 pain triggered by touch, and carbamazepine is first-line before any procedure.

Microvascular decompression with Teflon padding (Jannetta) suits young healthy patients with MRI-confirmed contact, while balloon compression, glycerol or Gamma Knife suit the elderly and MS-related cases.
Deep brain stimulation of STN or GPi smooths motor fluctuations in levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease after 5 years of therapy, and Vim stimulation controls essential tremor and dystonic tremor.

GPi stimulation treats generalised dystonia including DYT1 children, intrathecal baclofen pumps manage diffuse spasticity, and selective dorsal rhizotomy suits spastic diplegic cerebral palsy with good strength.

modules.name: Peripheral Nerve, Entrapments and Neurocutaneous Syndromes

topics.book: Sunderland nerve injury classification; AANEM entrapment guidance; NF/TSC diagnostic criteria

mustKnow.fact: Seddon-Sunderland grades run neurapraxia (I, conduction block, full recovery) through axonotmesis (II-IV, axon lost, Tinel advancing 1 mm per day) to neurotmesis (V, transection needing repair).
Nerve repair is done within days for clean cuts and before 6 months for closed injuries, with grafts bridging gaps above 2 to 3 cm, since motor endplates vanish after 12 to 18 denervated months.
Carpal tunnel gives night pain with Phalen and Tinel signs then thenar wasting, confirmed on nerve conduction, and transverse carpal ligament release cures most cases.
Ulnar cubital compression gives clawing with Froment sign, Erb C5-C6 gives waiter tip, and Klumpke C8-T1 gives medial hand claw with Horner syndrome from T1 sympathetic injury.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple (brachial plexus)

mustKnow.fact: Bell palsy is a lower motor neuron facial palsy involving the forehead with hyperacusis and taste loss, treated with steroids within 72 hours plus eye care, with 70 percent full recovery.
NF1 needs 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots plus Lisch nodules, optic glioma or neurofibromas, while NF2 gives bilateral vestibular schwannomas with merlin loss and LZTR1 marks schwannomatosis.
Tuberous sclerosis shows angiofibromas, shagreen patches and cortical tubers with infantile spasms treated by vigabatrin, and SEGA tumours shrink with everolimus.

Sturge-Weber gives V1 port-wine stain with tram-track calcification and leptomeningeal angioma causing seizures, and VHL combines haemangioblastoma with renal cancer and phaeochromocytoma needing staged resection.
